Title: The Week the Justice Department Tried to Referee the Election It Was Supposed to Protect
Content:
```markdown In the final eight days before the midterm elections, the machinery of federal law enforcement turned with unusual directness toward the election itself. Over the course of the week, the Department of Justice pressured election officials in at least five states, sued to block certification of a Senate race before it was even decided, and dispatched roughly a thousand officials to polling places nationwide. Courts intervened repeatedly, a congressional report alleged presidential misconduct stretching back decades, and early voters turned out in numbers that had already broken records by Friday morning. None of it resolved by week's end; it all arrived at Election Day still unsettled.

The week opened with two foreign-entanglement stories that, on their own, would have dominated most news cycles. President Trump waived congressionally mandated sanctions on the Russian energy firm Novatek two days before they were set to take effect, clearing the way for a Russian-backed stake in an Alaska liquefied natural gas project and prompting resignations inside the executive branch. At nearly the same time, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed a resource-extraction agreement granting the United States a 35 percent stake in a venture tied to a Venezuelan oligarch accused of money laundering, structured through an offshore shell company. Both arrangements raised immediate questions about oversight and foreign financial entanglement, but they were soon overtaken by a more sustained story: the opening moves of the Justice Department's campaign against state election administration.

That campaign began over the same weekend, when the administration sued Alaska in an apparent effort to preserve the option of blocking certification of a competitive Senate race, and the Justice Department separately demanded that California verify 20,000 ballots within 48 hours using a list that state officials called unreliable. A county clerk refused to comply, citing dozens of factual errors in the federal data. It was an unusually aggressive opening position, and it would not be the administration's last word on the matter — not by a wide margin. Meanwhile, at rallies in Georgia, Michigan, and elsewhere, the president dismissed public concern about gas prices, made crude remarks about a sitting senator, and leveled Islamophobic and antisemitic attacks against Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, suggesting he should pass through a metal detector before entering the Senate. Away from the campaign trail, the New York archdiocese finalized an $800 million settlement with more than 1,300 clergy abuse survivors, and a detainee died in ICE custody amid a hunger strike — the sixtieth such death recorded during the administration's tenure.

By Monday, the week's character as one dominated by information control and institutional pressure had sharpened. President Trump, following a DHS raid on her home, demanded that Rep. Ilhan Omar resign and then falsely told a rally crowd that she had conceded her seat, a claim with no basis in fact. The White House, separately, released video and photographs from a private Oval Office prayer session with Catholic bishops without their knowledge or consent, prompting a public apology from one archbishop, who called the release political manipulation ahead of the election. The Justice Department, for its part, announced charges against 48 noncitizens for alleged election crimes across five states, even as a second deceptive mailer campaign — funneled through an undisclosed shell entity — surfaced attacking Minnesota's Democratic gubernatorial nominee, echoing a similar operation already underway in Wisconsin. In Ohio, the Ramaswamy campaign released an advertisement featuring gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton's estranged mother disputing Acton's account of childhood abuse, despite court records confirming both the abuse and her removal from the home; the ad drew bipartisan condemnation and a surge of donations to Acton's campaign.

Tuesday brought the week's first major turn on two separate institutional fronts. House Judiciary Committee Democrats released a staff report compiling accounts from eleven women connected to Jeffrey Epstein's circle, five of whom accused President Trump of rape or sexual assault, including a new allegation from a former Miss Switzerland finalist describing an assault at a 1993 pageant. The report further alleged that Attorney General Todd Blanche had directed a witness not to discuss claims implicating the president, and it called for appointment of an independent special counsel given doubts about the Justice Department's willingness to investigate its own leadership. This was a distinct institutional story from the election-pressure campaign, running on a separate track through Congress rather than through the courts, but it added to a week already freighted with questions about accountability at the top of government.

On the election front, the Ninth Circuit ruled 2–1 against the Justice Department's bid to segregate the 20,000 California ballots, and a federal judge in a separate matter found that a Trump-appointed interim U.S. attorney had been serving unlawfully without Senate confirmation, disqualifying him from two pending prosecutions. The same day, the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act" took full effect, extracting roughly $1 trillion from the healthcare system primarily through Medicaid cuts expected to close rural and urban hospitals alike — the largest federal healthcare reduction in the nation's history. The Justice Department also pressed, and lost, a series of cases seeking nationwide access to state voter files, while attempting separately to use the Postal Service to screen ballots across the country; President Trump announced a $1 million reward for reports of voter fraud despite the absence of evidence of widespread fraud. North Carolina's election board removed on-campus polling sites from four universities, including the nation's largest historically Black college, and at least 18 rural Alaska polling locations failed to open as scheduled. Abroad, a student-led democratic movement in Serbia removed President Aleksandar Vučić, a close ally of Vladimir Putin, from power, and state television subsequently apologized for years of biased coverage — a pointed counterexample from outside the country's borders.

Wednesday continued the pattern of judicial rebuke. A federal district judge again rejected the Justice Department's attempt to force California to set aside ballots, ruling that the claims rested on unreliable data; the Justice Department appealed immediately. Separately, Representatives Robert Garcia and Jamie Raskin pressed Meta to explain the suspension of the "No Kings" Instagram account during get-out-the-vote rallies, part of what they described as a broader pattern of technical outages disproportionately affecting the president's political opponents; Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon reported her own Instagram account had been taken down mid-rally. Reports also surfaced of AI-generated disinformation proliferating across social media platforms as content moderation weakened, even as OpenAI announced an Election Operations Center intended to counter misinformation. Coverage of the House Judiciary report continued, and a federal judge granted a temporary restraining order blocking the Office of Management and Budget from funding government advertisements found likely to disadvantage Democratic candidates in competitive races.

Thursday marked the clearest turning point of the week on the election-interference thread. Judge David Carter rejected the Justice Department's ballot-segregation demand in California for a third time, this time explicitly finding that the administration had engaged in a "broad, ongoing pattern" of interference and noting that similar pressure letters had been sent to New Jersey, Nevada, and Pennsylvania. The Ninth Circuit dismissed the department's jurisdictional appeal the same day, and Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security to disclose, by noon the following day, every state in which they had pressured election officials to remove voters or withhold ballots. The department, undeterred, sent letters to election officials in all fifty states warning of possible criminal prosecution for violations of federal election law — despite a judge's prior warning to cease such threats — and sent Washington state a list of 405 allegedly ineligible voters that state officials found riddled with errors, including the names of actual U.S. citizens. In Nevada, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin's public claim that nearly 16,000 noncitizens appeared on the state's voter rolls quietly shrank to 185 names, all of whom were subsequently confirmed to be citizens.

The Alaska dispute, meanwhile, escalated sharply. President Trump called for Senate candidate Mary Peltola's removal from the ballot and her prosecution over a legal ballot-stacking tactic common to both parties, while Attorney General Blanche characterized the maneuver as "cheating" and "fraud" in a television interview. Alaska's Republican governor ordered a criminal investigation into Peltola's campaign without identifying any actual illegality. Separately, a transparency nonprofit released personal data belonging to more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors, exposing details of the agency's own surveillance programs even as DHS pursued efforts to unmask its critics and journalists covering it.

By Friday, the Alaska dispute reached its culmination: President Trump personally directed the Justice Department to sue to block certification of Alaska's Senate election if the Republican candidate lost, formalizing demands he had made publicly just a day earlier. In a separate but related gesture regarding electoral legitimacy abroad, Trump ordered the State Department to grant temporary humanitarian status to Flávio Bolsonaro, son of Brazil's defeated former president, with officials indicating that permanent residency would likely follow — a decision that, paired with the Alaska lawsuit, suggested a consistent willingness to treat election outcomes as negotiable when they ran counter to political preference.

The Justice Department's activity reached its broadest scale on Friday as well. Approximately 1,000 federal officials were dispatched to polling places nationwide, with county clerks in several states noting that deployments appeared concentrated in Hispanic-majority, Democratic-leaning areas. The same day, the department opened criminal investigations into California election officials, issued subpoenas, and threatened further litigation against Washington state over its ballot procedures. Against this backdrop, more than 46 million Americans had already cast early ballots by Friday morning, surpassing the entire early-vote total of the 2022 midterms, with notable surges in Texas, Michigan, North Carolina, and Kansas — a marker of civic engagement undiminished, at least in turnout terms, by the surrounding pressure.

The week closed with several other threads still unresolved. A federal judge issued a preliminary injunction blocking the removal of trees at Washington's East Park for a planned redesign of a Trump golf course, after finding the project was real despite earlier denials, and a grand jury declined to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over her January 6th testimony. Reporting revealed that ICE had conducted one of the largest anti-left surveillance operations in the nation's history and that roughly 100 immigration judges had been fired since the start of the administration, with one judge alleging direct pressure over how to rule. President Trump suggested without evidence that Brazilian President Lula's decisively won and internationally recognized election victory had been rigged, and, in an unrelated exchange about a leak investigation, used incorrect gendered language to threaten a male military officer. Quietly, state officials began preparing for contingencies of their own: Maryland's election administrator disclosed that he had made plans for his own potential arrest on Election Day, and Michigan's attorney general described drafting legal briefs to address nearly every conceivable scenario of federal interference.

Taken as a whole, the week recorded a sustained and escalating effort by federal law enforcement to intervene in state-run elections in the days immediately preceding a national vote, met at nearly every turn by judicial rulings that described the effort in increasingly pointed terms — unprecedented coercion, a broad and ongoing pattern, interference requiring disclosure under court order. It also recorded a parallel and separate reckoning, carried by Congress rather than the courts, over allegations reaching the presidency itself. Neither thread reached a final resolution by week's end. What the week did make clear was the scale of institutional friction generated when federal power is directed at the machinery of elections rather than left to the states and courts that ordinarily administer them, and the extent to which courts, state officials, and voters themselves continued to function as checks against that pressure even as it intensified. ```
